sections.title: Mediating the Americas
sections.description:
This course examines how media industries, histories and objects, cultural policies, audiences, and workers have shaped political, economic, and ideological exchanges among nations and regions across the Americas. Particular attention will be given to media as instruments of both control and resistance in relation to U.S. foreign policy in Latin America over the past two centuries.
Topics include competing hemispheric imaginaries of the Americas; media imperialism and cultural exchange between North and South America; Cold War cultural geopolitics and national and regional media practices; the effects of NAFTA and other free-trade policies on Latin American media industries; and the rise and decline of Latin American media capitals in relation to these political and economic transformations.
The course also considers how media regions are defined and redefined through geopolitical transformations, imperialism, and globalization, generating new areas and objects of research that illuminate the changing contours of media exchange. It engages key texts and critical perspectives in cultural studies and media theory emerging from Latin America.
Through the study of film, television, radio, and digital media, the course emphasizes historiographical questions concerning the formation of the American hemisphere through political economies, cultural agency and production, repression and resistance, activism, violence, technological and cultural exchange, institutional infrastructures, and free trade.
